title: Baseline monocyte GIP receptor mRNA expression is associated with reductions in body weight and FIB-4 index after switching to tirzepatide in patients with type 2 diabetes.
abstract: Tirzepatide improves body weight and glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes, but factors associated with inter-individual differences after switching remain unclear. We examined whether baseline monocyte glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor (GIPR) mRNA expression was associated with changes in body weight and the fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index after switching from glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) to tirzepatide. This single-center retrospective study included 90 patients with type 2 diabetes who had received a GLP-1RA for at least 6 months before switching. Baseline monocyte GIPR mRNA expression was measured by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction. Associations with percentage body-weight change and FIB-4 index change during the 6 months after tirzepatide initiation were assessed by correlation and multivariable regression. Exploratory ex vivo assays were performed to assess monocyte responses to native GIP. Higher baseline monocyte GIPR mRNA expression was associated with greater reductions in body weight and the FIB-4 index and remained significant in multivariable models. The association with the FIB-4 index remained significant after additional adjustment for percentage body-weight change at 6 months after tirzepatide initiation. GIPR mRNA expression was not associated with body-weight change during the preceding 6 months of GLP-1RA therapy. Native GIP suppressed lipopolysaccharide-induced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha responses in monocytes. Baseline monocyte GIPR mRNA expression was associated with body-weight and FIB-4 index reductions after switching to tirzepatide. It may represent an exploratory marker of clinical changes, but treatment specificity, causal GIPR-dependent mechanisms, and structural liver fibrosis regression were not established. Summary of the study design and main finding. Baseline GIPR mRNA expression in peripheral blood monocytes was associated with reductions in body weight and the FIB-4 index after switching to tirzepatide in patients with type 2 diabetes. In exploratory ex vivo assays, native GIP suppressed LPS-induced inflammatory responses, supporting monocyte GIPR expression as a candidate exploratory marker requiring further validation. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13340-026-00940-3.

title: AA in Obesity and Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD) Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD).
journal: Reviews of physiology, biochemistry and pharmacology
abstract: Obesity and MASLD (NAFLD) are chronic, low-grade systemic inflammatory diseases resulting from complex interactions among diet, adipose tissue, gut microbiota, liver, muscle, pancreas, and the brain. Central to this integrative framework are AA and other polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), which regulate inflammation, insulin sensitivity, neuroendocrine signaling, and energy homeostasis.Excess consumption of energy-dense foods rich in saturated and trans fats leads to adipocyte hypertrophy, altered membrane fluidity, increased antigenicity, and enhanced recruitment of macrophages and T cells into adipose tissue. These changes promote the sustained release of pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IL-6, MIF, and CRP, contributing to insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, and MASLD (NAFLD). In contrast, adequate availability of GLA, DGLA, AA, EPA, and DHA improves cell membrane dynamics and serves as a substrate for anti-inflammatory and pro-resolving lipid mediators, including lipoxins, resolvins, protectins, maresins, and nitrolipids, which suppress inflammatory signaling and enhance adiponectin production.Abdominal obesity can be considered a localized glucocorticoid excess state driven by increased adipose 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase-1 (11β-HSD-1) activity, linking visceral fat accumulation to insulin resistance, altered PPAR signaling, and chronic inflammation. Suppression of 11β-HSD-1, increased PUFA intake, and exercise can ameliorate these abnormalities.Gut microbiota and their short-chain fatty acids influence inflammation, leptin signaling, incretin secretion, and lipid metabolism, while PUFAs-including AA-activate gut-brain-liver neural circuits via vagal pathways and G protein-coupled receptors to regulate satiety, insulin secretion, and hepatic glucose production. This chapter also emphasizes the role of hypothalamic factors, particularly BDNF, in integrating nutritional, hormonal, and inflammatory signals.In summary, AA and related PUFAs are critical modulators of inflammation resolution, neuroendocrine control, and metabolic balance, offering a unifying mechanistic framework for the prevention and management of obesity and its associated metabolic disorders.

title: Immunometabolic regulation of macrophage function in cardio-hepatic-renal comorbidities: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: This review examines metabolic comorbidities affecting the heart, liver and kidney. The clinical prevalence of cardiohepatorenal metabolic comorbidities associated with obesity and type 2 diabetes is substantial. Chronic low-grade inflammation serves as the fundamental pathogenic mechanism. Abnormal macrophage activation is associated with metabolic disorders and damage to multiple organs. The conventional M1/M2 binary classification fails to adequately capture the heterogeneity of macrophages in vivo. Previous studies have primarily focused on the investigation of individual organs, leaving the cross-organ immune-metabolic linkage mechanism poorly understood. Furthermore, targeted interventions often lack precision. In this study, we systematically summarize the roles of macrophage polarization, phenotypic remodeling and metabolic activation in the injury of three metabolic organs. We also analyze their mediating functions in inter-organ immune-metabolic crosstalk and the associated pathological connections. Glycolipid toxicity impairs the glycolipid metabolism of macrophages via the NLRP3/SIRT pathway, resulting in a pro-inflammatory polarization advantage. Specific subsets of macrophages, including CCR2+,TREM2+,and CD206+CD68+,are involved in mediating myocardial remodeling, liver fibrosis, and renal interstitial injury, respectively.Medications such as SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists may provide multi-organ protection by modulating macrophage activity. The current research presents several limitations, including species differences between humans and mice, ambiguous temporal transformation rules of macrophages, and inadequate specificity of targeted preparations.Future efforts should leverage spatial multi-omics and gene editing technologies to analyze the global regulatory network and develop highly selective targeted strategies. This approach can offer theoretical support for the integrated and precise prevention and management of metabolic comorbidities.

title: Gut microbiome-targeted bile acid metabolomics integration reveals dietary cordycepin alleviates NAFLD in diabetic mice by enriching Clostridia and affecting the PXR/Sult2a1/CA7S.
abstract: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) frequently coexists with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), posing a significant metabolic disorder with limited dietary intervention options. Cordycepin, a food‑derived nucleoside from the edible fungus Cordyceps militaris, exhibits hypoglycemic and hypolipidemic effects, but its role in T2DM combined with NAFLD remains unknown. Here, we established a mouse model of T2DM combined with NAFLD in male KM mice using high-fructose and high‑fat diet, and streptozotocin. Both cordycepin (COR) and C. militaris water extract (CWE) attenuated glucose intolerance, dyslipidemia, hepatic steatosis, liver injury, inflammatory response and oxidative stress, with cordycepin showing superior efficacy. Multi‑omics analysis revealed that cordycepin uniquely reshaped the gut microbiota by significantly enriching the c__Clostridia, including g__Acetatifactor, g__Anaerovorax, g__Monoglobus, s__Acutalibacter_muris, and further affected liver metabolism, which was characterized by enrichment of bile acid metabolism-related pathways. Targeted bile acid metabolomics demonstrated that cordycepin specifically promoted the production of cholic acid‑7‑sulfate (CA7S), a gut‑restricted secondary bile acid, through activation of the hepatic PXR/Sult2a1 pathway. Notably, integrated correlation analysis revealed a significant positive association between CA7S and c__Clostridia (e.g., g__Monoglobus, g__Lachnoclostridium, and g__Anaerovorax), suggesting that cordycepin enhances CA7S production by enriching these Clostridia members. And CA7S activated TGR5 to stimulate glucagon‑like peptide‑1 (GLP‑1) secretion, thereby improving glucose and lipid homeostasis. Therefore, these findings demonstrate that dietary cordycepin improves T2DM combined with NAFLD by modulating gut microbiota, particularly Clostridia, and affecting the PXR/Sult2a1/CA7S/GLP‑1 pathway, thereby exerting beneficial effects on glucose and lipid homeostasis.

title: Mulberry leaf flavonoids alleviate type 2 diabetes by remodeling the gut microbiota-bile acid axis and activating FXR signaling.
abstract: Mulberry leaf (Morus alba L.) has long been used in traditional Chinese medicine for treating "Xiaoke" (diabetes), as documented in "Compendium of Materia Medica" compiled by Li Shi-Zhen of the Ming Dynasty. Mulberry leaf flavonoids (MLF) are the major active components and have demonstrated anti-diabetic effects in modern studies. However, whether MLF alleviates type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) by modulating the gut microbiota-bile acid axis and directly activating key metabolic receptors such as FXR remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate whether MLF ameliorates T2DM through remodeling the gut microbiota-bile acid axis and activating FXR signaling, and to identify potential flavonoid constituents within MLF that directly interact with FXR. db/db mice were treated with low- or high-dose MLF (300 or 600 mg/kg/day) or metformin for 10 weeks. Blood glucose, insulin sensitivity, lipid profiles, and hepatic pathology were assessed. Gut microbiota composition was analyzed by 16S rRNA sequencing, and bile acid profiles in serum, liver, ileum, and feces were quantified by targeted metabolomics. The expression of FXR/TGR5 signaling pathway components was determined by qRT-PCR and Western blot. Molecular docking was performed to screen for potential FXR modulator among MLF constituents, followed by in vitro validation using HepG2 and Caco-2 cells. MLF treatment significantly reduced fasting blood glucose, improved glucose tolerance and insulin resistance, lowered serum and hepatic lipid levels, and alleviated hepatic steatosis in db/db mice. MLF reshaped the gut microbiota by increasing beneficial genera (e.g., Alloprevotella, Roseburia) and decreasing the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio. Concurrently, MLF reprogrammed bile acid profiles across multiple organs, elevating non-12-OH bile acids (e.g., CDCA) and reducing the FXR antagonist Tβ-MCA, thereby activating intestinal and hepatic FXR/TGR5 signaling, upregulating FGF15 and SHP, and increasing serum GLP-1. Molecular docking identified Morusin as a candidate FXR ligand, and in vitro assays confirmed that both MLF and Morusin activated FXR and modulated downstream targets (BSEP, NTCP, ASBT, CYP7A1) in hepatocytes and intestinal cells. MLF alleviates T2DM by remodeling the gut microbiota-bile acid axis and activating FXR/TGR5 signaling. Morusin, a flavonoid constituent of MLF, is a potential FXR-modulating compound. These findings provide a modern mechanistic rationale for the traditional use of mulberry leaf in treating diabetes and support the development of MLF as a gut-targeted therapeutic strategy for T2DM.

title: Annualized fibrosis dynamics in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease: a paired-biopsy cohort.
abstract: Fibrosis stage is the strongest histologic determinant of outcomes in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), but annualized fibrosis dynamics under routine care remain insufficiently quantified. We characterized fibrosis progression rate (FPR) in a long-term, pre-incretin paired-biopsy cohort to provide reference data for emerging metabolic therapies. We analyzed 153 patients with MASLD who underwent repeat liver biopsy at a single center over a median interval of 5.9 years (range, 0.5-24). No patient received a GLP-1 receptor agonist or a dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist during follow-up. FPR was defined as the annualized change in fibrosis stage (stage/year). Factors associated with fibrosis improvement were examined using multivariable logistic regression. Fibrosis improved in 38 patients (25%), remained stable in 66 (43%), and progressed in 49 (32%). FPR varied substantially among patients with improvement or progression, revealing bidirectional and heterogeneous fibrosis dynamics not captured by categorical staging alone. FPR shifted in parallel with MASLD activity score change and was more closely related to changes in hepatocellular ballooning and lobular inflammation than to steatosis. Male sex, advanced baseline fibrosis, and ≥5% body weight reduction were associated with fibrosis improvement, with the likelihood increasing as these factors accumulated. In this real-world pre-incretin paired-biopsy cohort, fibrosis change under routine care was bidirectional and heterogeneous, with wide variation in annualized rate. These data provide a reference for evaluating how emerging metabolic therapies modify the longitudinal course of MASLD.

title: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease: Pathogenesis, complications and pharmacological treatment.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is increasing in prevalence worldwide. Pathogenesis of MASLD has been considerably heterogenous. Increased hepatic de novo lipogenesis, adipose tissue dysfunction, genetic predisposition, epigenetic mechanism, and other related factors have been associated with the development and progression of MASLD. Patients with MASLD are at high risk of not only adverse liver-related outcomes, including hepatocellular carcinoma, but also cardiometabolic disease including type 2 diabetes mellitus. Weight loss is the cornerstone of therapy among the various treatments for MASLD to decrease hepatic fat accumulation and delay the progression of inflammation and fibrosis. Resmetirom and semaglutide are approved for the treatment of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis with moderate to advanced fibrosis, and many drugs are under investigation. Careful attention should be paid to the screening of MASLD, and concerted efforts should be made to manage it appropriately. See also the graphical abstract(Fig. 1).

title: Type 2 diabetes and the cardio-renal-metabolic syndrome: The evolving roles of GLP-1 and dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists.
abstract: The impact of type 2 diabetes (T2D) extends beyond mere management of blood glucose; it also encompasses related cardiovascular, renal and metabolic issues. This interconnected framework, known as the cardio-renal-metabolic (CRM) syndrome, calls for a shift in therapeutic approach. While traditional treatments have made progress focusing on glucose management, a residual risk still exists for conditions such as atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, heart failure and obesity. The 2025 American Diabetes Association Standards of Care now emphasize treatment algorithms based on risk and complication management, prioritizing comorbidities associated with the CRM syndrome rather than solely focusing on glucose management. This article consolidates current evidence, mechanistic insights and clinical trial findings that support the use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and the dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonist to reduce CRM risk. We examine key cardiovascular and renal outcomes trials, as well as metabolic-related trials, such as weight loss and the management of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), and their alignment with guideline-directed care. In addition to efficacy and safety, we also focus on addressing disparities in access and overcoming implementation challenges, such as low use among specific subpopulations. Lastly, we explore the future of incretin-based therapies, including new triple agonists and ongoing research. Prompt and equitable adoption of GLP-1-based therapeutic options could improve the standard of care for T2D by addressing the entire range of CRM syndrome.

title: Gut microbiota and treatment response heterogeneity across pharmacological therapies for MASH.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a progressive liver disease with increasing global prevalence. However, substantial inter-individual variability in therapeutic response remains a major challenge for effective disease management. Although the gut microbiota is well recognized as a key contributor to MASH pathogenesis, its role in shaping pharmacological treatment response remains insufficiently understood and underexplored in clinical contexts. In this Review, we summarize evidence suggesting that gut microbiota-associated metabolites, including bile acids, short-chain fatty acids, sphingolipids, and other microbial products, may contribute to variability in therapeutic response across major pharmacological classes for MASH, including FXR agonists, PPAR agonists, FGF19/FGF21 analogues, thyroid hormone receptor-β agonists, and incretin-based therapies. However, for most therapeutic classes, direct clinical evidence linking microbiota features to inter-individual treatment response remains limited, and much of the mechanistic evidence is derived from preclinical studies. We integrate current evidence into a response-oriented conceptual framework linking microbiome composition and metabolic activity to biological processes relevant to drug efficacy. This framework identifies priorities for the prospective validation of microbiome-derived biomarkers and microbiome-informed patient stratification in MASH.

title: Complication Prevention Beyond Glycaemic Control in Type 2 Diabetes: Cumulative Metabolic Exposure, Organ Vulnerability and Treatment Durability.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes is a progressive multisystem disorder in which long-term complication burden reflects more than contemporaneous glycaemic control. Age at onset, previous metabolic exposure, obesity-related risk, organ injury, treatment safety and the capacity to sustain effective care interact across the disease course. This critical narrative review synthesised targeted PubMed/MEDLINE searches, international guidance, landmark and contemporary randomised trials, longitudinal cohorts, validated risk models and clinically influential reviews. A targeted update search was completed through 22 September 2026. The evidence supports a clinically ordered approach in which immediate treatment-related hazards are considered first, followed by established organ disease or a dominant preventable outcome, residual modifiable cardiometabolic exposure, treatment durability and the care systems required to translate evidence into sustained benefit. Historical trials established the importance of glycaemic, blood-pressure and lipid management and coordinated multifactorial intervention. Contemporary SGLT2 inhibitor and incretin-based trials add direct cardiovascular, heart-failure and kidney outcome evidence in defined populations, while MASH trials provide emerging histological evidence. HbA1c, validated risk equations and organ-specific pathways retain their established roles. The proposed framework is interpretive rather than predictive. It does not assign numerical weights or treatment thresholds but aims to identify the preventable outcome that should take priority, the intervention supported by the most relevant evidence and whether that intervention can be implemented safely and durably.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Versus Empagliflozin or Dapagliflozin in the MASLD-Heart Failure Phenotype: An Exploratory Propensity-Matched Cohort Study.
abstract: Treatment selection may confound observational comparisons of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and heart failure (HF). To compare recorded outcomes between treatment groups and examine whether the associations persisted after restricting the analysis by agent and diabetes status and separating early and later outcome windows. Retrospective, initiation-based, active-comparator cohort study (new-user design not verified). We used the TriNetX US Collaborative Network and a common index eligibility period from January 1, 2018, through June 2, 2026. The revised analyses were performed on September 12, 2026. An additional sensitivity analysis of acute HF excluded patients with this outcome before the start of the day 1-1825 window. The primary analysis compared semaglutide, liraglutide, or dulaglutide with empagliflozin or dapagliflozin using 1:1 propensity score matching and assessed outcomes during days 1-1825. Separate analyses of the broader GLP-1 RA group examined outcomes during days 1-90 and 91-1825 and among patients with type 2 diabetes and no recorded type 1 diabetes. We report endpoint-specific event proportions, risk differences, hazard ratios (HRs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and proportionality test results. The primary analysis included 8,550 patients per group after matching. Mortality occurred in 599/8,514 (7.0%) versus 861/8,509 (10.1%); the HR was 0.607 (95% CI, 0.546-0.673). Coded acute HF diagnoses occurred in 1,217/8,550 (14.2%) versus 2,525/8,550 (29.5%); the HR was 0.398 (95% CI, 0.372-0.427), with evidence of non-proportional hazards. In separately matched descriptive interval analyses (8,489 patients per group), the HR for coded acute HF was 0.262 (95% CI, 0.236-0.291) during days 1-90 and 0.507 (95% CI, 0.469-0.548) during days 91-1825. The HR for acute kidney injury during the later interval was 0.740 (95% CI, 0.650-0.842). Among 5,709 matched pairs with type 2 diabetes and no recorded type 1 diabetes, the HR for coded acute HF was 0.431 (95% CI, 0.397-0.468), whereas the HR for ketoacidosis was 0.683 (95% CI, 0.455-1.025). No advantage was observed for acute pancreatitis in any analysis. In a separate analysis excluding patients with prior acute HF, the HR was 0.421 (95% CI, 0.362-0.489), with evidence of non-proportional hazards. Albumin and bilirubin remained imbalanced in a direction favoring the GLP-1 RA group; body mass index also remained imbalanced. GLP-1 RA exposure was associated with lower observed hazards for several outcomes, and the association with coded acute HF was weaker after day 90. The early concentration and magnitude of this association make treatment channeling a plausible explanation, although this analysis cannot establish that explanation. These exploratory findings do not support causal inferences or treatment-preference conclusions and do not challenge randomized evidence supporting SGLT2i use in HF.

title: Association of GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy with cardiovascular outcomes in patients with MASLD: A translational study.
abstract: Patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) are at increased risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes, potentially involving systemic metabolic dysfunction and cardiac remodeling. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) improve metabolic dysfunction in MASLD; however, their associations with cardiovascular outcomes and effects on MASLD-associated cardiac remodeling remain incompletely understood. In this translational study, we integrated a real-world TriNetX cohort of patients with MASLD and T2D with complementary experimental studies in a mouse model of MASLD. Following propensity score matching, 42,910 patients were included in each treatment group. GLP-1 RA therapy was associated with a lower risk of the primary composite cardiovascular outcome compared with sulfonylurea therapy (hazard ratio 0.87, 95% confidence interval 0.84-0.91; P < 0.001), although this association was not statistically significant in 90-day and 180-day landmark analyses. In Western diet-fed mice, GLP-1 RA treatment improved selected indices of cardiac function and attenuated cardiomyocyte hypertrophy. Although myocardial fibrosis was numerically reduced, the difference compared with vehicle-treated mice was not statistically significant (P = 0.28). Molecular analyses showed reduced expression of fibrosis- and extracellular matrix remodeling-related markers, including CTGF, TGF-β1, and vimentin. Collectively, GLP-1 RA therapy was associated with lower cardiovascular risk in the primary observational analysis, although this finding was not consistently supported by sensitivity analyses. Complementary experimental findings suggest improvements in selected cardiac functional indices and changes in fibrosis-associated molecular remodeling, warranting further investigation.

title: From pathophysiology to therapy: dual and triple agonists as a new frontier in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) has emerged as the most prevalent chronic liver condition worldwide, reflecting the growing global burden of obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D). The complex pathophysiology of MASLD, characterized by insulin resistance (IR), lipotoxicity, and chronic low-grade inflammation, necessitates therapeutic strategies that address systemic metabolic dysfunction rather than isolated hepatic markers. Current evidence highlights the synergistic potential of targeting multiple incretin and metabolic pathways. Dual agonists, most notably Tirzepatide (a GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist), have demonstrated profound efficacy in clinical trials (SURPASS and SURMOUNT programs), achieving significant reductions in hemoglobin A1c, body weight, and liver fat content. Furthermore, dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonists like Survodutide and Cotadutide offer complementary benefits by enhancing energy expenditure and modulating hepatic lipid metabolism. The development of triple agonists, such as Retatrutide (targeting GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors), represents a further escalation in potency, showing unprecedented results in liver fat reduction and weight loss. The integration of these multi-target agents, together with emerging pathways involving amylin analogues and pan-PPAR agonists like Chiglitazar, marks a paradigm shift toward holistic cardiometabolic management. These therapies not only target the resolution of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and fibrosis but also address the interconnected risks of cardiovascular and renal complications. This review aims to explore the evolving landscape of pharmacological interventions, focusing on the emergence of dual and triple receptor agonists as a transformative frontier in metabolic dysfunction and MASLD therapy.

title: Normal-BMI MASLD is Associated with Increased Mortality, Cardiovascular Events, Cancer and Lower GLP-1 Use.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) can occur in individuals who are not overweight or have obesity (normal-BMI MASLD), yet disease burden and management remain poorly characterized. We compared long-term outcomes and incretin-based therapy use between normal-BMI MASLD (nbMASLD) and overweight/obesity-associated MASLD (obMASLD) across racial and ethnic groups. We conducted a retrospective, observational study using the TriNetX United States Network. Adults diagnosed with MASLD or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) from 2005-2025 were classified using ethnicity-informed normal-BMI thresholds: <23 kg/m2 for Asian, <27 kg/m2 for Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander, and <25 kg/m2 for White/others. Propensity-score matching balanced demographic and clinical covariates. Outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analyses and Cox proportional hazards models with obMASLD as the reference group. Among 619,171 eligible patients, 51,940 matched pairs were identified. Nb-BMI MASLD was associated with higher all-cause mortality across grouped ethnic groups, with survival of 77.49% versus 83.93% in obMASLD (HR 1.735, CI 1.653-1.822). Ethnicity-specific risks included higher myocardial infarction risk in White and Black patients, higher stroke risk in White patients, higher ESRD risk in Black patients, and increased cancers (colorectal, pancreatic and multiple myeloma) among White patients. Incretin-based therapy (IBT) use was markedly lower in nbMASLD but was associated with improved survival. Patients with nbMASLD demonstrated an increased mortality and ethnicity-specific clinical complications than obMASLD despite a more favorable metabolic profile. These findings demonstrate a potential treatment gap for nbMASLD patients and the shortcomings of BMI-based strategies to risk-stratify MASLD patients.

title: Semaglutide for MASH in Japanese patients: findings consistent with the overall ESSENCE population.
Combination Therapy Potential of HTD1801 (Berberine Ursodeoxycholate) in MASLD/MASH and Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Disease: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Background/Objectives: The cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) continuum is characterized by the close interrelatedness of metabolic, hepatic, cardiovascular, and renal disease, making multidomain therapies particularly relevant to MASLD/MASH. HTD1801, an investigational ionic therapeutic, combines berberine's metabolic effects with the hepatoprotective effects of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), making it a potential multidomain therapy within this setting. This review had two related goals: first, to synthesize the mechanistic and clinical evidence for HTD1801 itself; and second, to evaluate the rationale and available evidence for extending this complementary-action approach through combination with other therapies relevant to MASLD/MASH and CKM disease. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, conference abstracts, and selected regulatory or sponsor sources were reviewed through 9 August 2026. Six CKM-relevant therapeutic classes were selected for their human evidence of multidomain benefit: metformin, GLP-1 receptor agonists, statins, SGLT2 inhibitors, PPAR agonists, and resmetirom. Studies of both HTD1801 and its individual components, berberine and UDCA, were included. A systematic review or meta-analysis was not feasible due to the limited and heterogeneous evidence base, instead necessitatinganarrative review. Results: Across seven completed HTD1801 clinical studies with publicly reported results, treatment showed multidomain metabolic and hepatic benefits across the CKM spectrum, including improvements in HbA1c, LDL-C, MRI-PDFF hepatic fat, ALT, AST, and GGT. Direct human evidence: HTD1801 + metformin, supported by a Phase 3 randomized add-on trial. Indirect human evidence: HTD1801 + SGLT2 inhibitors. Preclinical evidence: HTD1801 + GLP-1 receptor agonists; berberine + statins. Theoretical mechanistic rationale only: HTD1801 + PPAR agonists; HTD1801 + resmetirom. Overall, mechanistic and preclinical rationale has advanced further than direct human validation, and evidence remains centered largely on surrogate rather than definitive clinical outcomes. Conclusions: HTD1801 has demonstrated multidomain metabolic and hepatic activity, but direct human evidence supporting its use with other CKM therapies remains limited and is currently established only for metformin. The principal next step is to test HTD1801 in dedicated combination RCTs for clinically meaningful benefit. Further studies should characterize combination-specific safety and tolerability and compare HTD1801 with separate berberine and UDCA administration.

title: Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease and Steatohepatitis (MASLD/MASH) and Cardiovascular Risk: Emerging Therapeutic Strategies at the Interface of Liver and Cardiometabolic Disease.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and its progressive form, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), are increasingly recognized as systemic cardiometabolic disorders rather than isolated liver diseases. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) represents the leading cause of mortality in patients with MASLD/MASH, highlighting the need for therapeutic strategies that address both hepatic and cardiovascular risk. MASLD/MASH and CVD are connected through a network of interdependent mechanisms, including adipose tissue dysfunction, insulin resistance, altered insulin-glucagon signaling, atherogenic dyslipidemia, lipotoxicity, mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum stress, innate immune activation, chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, thrombogenic signaling, and dysregulated hepatokine and adipokine pathways. These mechanisms provide potential therapeutic entry points across the liver-adipose tissue-vascular axis. Lifestyle modification and conventional cardiometabolic therapies remain foundational, while several pharmacological agents increasingly target specific components of this network. We summarize the mechanistic rationale and clinical evidence for emerging therapies, including glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, dual incretin agonists, fibroblast growth factor 21 analogs, thyroid hormone receptor-β agonists, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor agonists, and agents targeting de novo lipogenesis. We further discuss why residual metabolic, inflammatory, and fibrogenic activity may limit monotherapy and how mechanism-based combination therapy could improve efficacy while mitigating treatment-related metabolic liabilities. Finally, we outline future priorities, including biomarker-guided patient selection, longitudinal noninvasive monitoring, integrated hepatic-cardiovascular trial endpoints, adaptive combination strategies, and development of therapies targeting immune, fibrogenic, and inter-organ signaling pathways.

title: Chronic Intermittent Hypoxia and MASLD in Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Critical Appraisal of Mechanistic and Causal Evidence.
abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) frequently coexist and share a common cardiometabolic substrate through a shared cardiometabolic substrate. This narrative review critically appraises the epidemiological, experimental, and interventional evidence proposed to link chronic intermittent hypoxia (CIH) and sleep fragmentation to hepatic steatosis, steatohepatitis, and fibrosis. We summarize the candidate mechanisms, including mitochondrial oxidative stress, hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha signaling, sympathetically driven lipolysis, and Kupffer and stellate cell activation and then examine the limits of the evidence supporting them: hypoxia-induced hypophagia and the scarcity of pair-fed controls in rodent models, species differences in the physiological response to hypoxia, publication bias, common-cause confounding by age and systemic inflammation, and the rarity of progressive liver disease in lean patients with anatomically driven OSA. We further review non-invasive diagnostic tools, polysomnographic hypoxemia indices, transient elastography, METS-IR, FIB-4, and emerging biomarkers, such as omentin-1 and follistatin-like 1, that enable bidirectional screening between sleep and hepatology clinics. Finally, we discuss therapeutic strategies, including continuous positive airway pressure, structured weight loss, and incretin-based pharmacotherapy (GLP-1 and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists), highlighting recent phase 3 evidence for tirzepatide in OSA and semaglutide in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis. Current evidence supports CIH as a context-dependent amplifier of liver injury in patients with pre-existing metabolic dysfunction rather than as an established independent cause of MASH. This interpretation still justifies integrated screening and treatment pathways, while identifying the study designs needed to test causality directly.

title: Efficacy and safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH): A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) are increasingly prevalent liver diseases closely linked to obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and cardiometabolic risk. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) may improve hepatic and metabolic outcomes through weight reduction, improved glycemic control, and reductions in hepatic steatosis. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of GLP-1 RAs in adults with MASLD or MASH. A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched for English-language studies published between January 2019 and December 2025. Eligible studies included adults with MASLD or MASH treated with GLP-1 RAs and reporting hepatic, metabolic, or safety outcomes. Pooled estimates were calculated using random-effects models. Nine studies involving 795 participants were included. GLP-1 RA therapy was associated with significant reductions in liver fat content (mean difference [MD]: -3.17; 95% CI: -4.06 to -2.29), body weight (MD: -4.68; 95% CI: -6.88 to -2.47), alanine aminotransferase (MD: -15.17; 95% CI: -21.29 to -9.05), aspartate aminotransferase (MD: -9.89; 95% CI: -13.65 to -6.13), and HbA1c (MD: -0.78; 95% CI: -1.07 to -0.49). Adverse events were more frequent with GLP-1 RAs, particularly nausea and vomiting, while serious adverse events did not differ significantly between groups. GLP-1 RAs are associated with meaningful improvements in hepatic steatosis, liver enzymes, body weight, and glycemic control in patients with MASLD or MASH. These findings support their potential role, particularly in patients with coexisting obesity or type 2 diabetes. However, further long-term, adequately powered trials are needed to clarify their effects on fibrosis regression, histological outcomes, and liver-related clinical events.

title: Fasting Hormonal and Inflammatory Profiles according to Liver Fibrosis Stages in Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease.
journal: American journal of physiology. Gastrointestinal and liver physiology
abstract: Endocrine mechanisms underlying progression of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) to advanced fibrosis remain unclear. We aimed to characterize fasting hepatokines, adipokines, gastrointestinal hormones, and inflammatory markers according to fibrosis stages in MASLD and explore their associations with glucose and lipid metabolism. In this cross-sectional study, 79 individuals with MASLD were grouped into no evidence of advanced fibrosis (no-AF; F0-F2) (n=51) and advanced fibrosis (AF; F3-F4) (n=28). Fasting plasma levels of hepatokines (ANGPTL3, ANGPTL4, ANGPTL6, and FGF-21), adipokines (leptin), gastrointestinal hormones (GLP-1, GIP, glucagon, and FGF-19), and inflammatory markers (TNF-α, IL-6, and MCP-1) were measured. Spearman correlations between hormones and indices of glucose and lipid metabolism were calculated and further adjusted for age, sex, and BMI. Median age (56[44-64] vs. 56[48-65] yr), sex (57 vs. 39% women), and BMI (33[27-37] vs. 34[31-38] kg/m2) were comparable between groups. Individuals with AF had lower ANGPTL6 (p=0.03) and higher IL-6 (p=0.02) and TNF-α (p<0.0001), whereas other hepatokines, leptin, and gastrointestinal hormones were similar between groups. Independently of age, sex, and BMI, ANGTL6 was positively associated with triglycerides (r=0.44, p<0.01). GIP and glucagon were strongly associated with hepatic and adipose tissue insulin resistance and reduced β-cell function (p≤0.003). Additionally, FGF-19 was negatively associated with hepatic insulin sensitivity (r=-0.26, p=0.02) and positively associated with insulin secretion (r=0.27, p=0.02). Overall, our results suggest that advanced fibrosis is characterized by selective reduction of ANGPTL6 and increased inflammatory markers rather than global endocrine alterations. Gastrointestinal hormones could be major contributors of impaired fasting glucose metabolism in MASLD.

title: Taiwan GEST-TASL-TMASO Joint Position Statement in Managing Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease and Obesity.
journal: Liver international : official journal of the International Association for the Study of the Liver
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and obesity share common pathogenesis and are increasingly relevant in clinical care. This joint statement addresses the need for comprehensive guidance in Taiwan for MASLD patients with obesity. The Gastroenterological Society of Taiwan, the Taiwan Association for the Study of the Liver, and the Taiwan Medical Association for the Study of Obesity conducted an evidence-based review, integrating epidemiological data, clinical trial outcomes, and expert consensus to develop position statements covering diagnosis, disease burden, pathogenesis, surveillance, and therapeutic strategies. MASLD prevalence in Taiwanese adults is 30%-45%, reaching 60%-70% in individuals with obesity, with similar high prevalence in children and adolescents. Obesity accelerates hepatic and extrahepatic disease progression, including cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and cardiovascular complications. Lifestyle interventions, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, resmetirom, and bariatric surgery demonstrate efficacy in improving hepatic and metabolic outcomes. Risk stratification using noninvasive tools such as Fibrosis-4 and vibration-controlled transient elastography effectively guides referral and management. A multidisciplinary, precision-based approach, integrating lifestyle modification, pharmacotherapy, surgical options, and risk stratification, is essential for effective MASLD management in patients with obesity, while research into artificial intelligence-driven biomarkers, gut microbiota modulation, and genetic factors represents future directions.

title: A rare diagnosis during evaluation for metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease: Glycogen storage disease type Ia presenting during adolescence in a male with severe obesity.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a common comorbidity of pediatric obesity that predisposes patients to hepatocellular adenomas (HCAs). HCAs however are nonspecific to MASLD and warrant further evaluation. We present a case of a 16-year-old male with severe obesity, and persistently elevated liver enzymes, initially evaluated for MASLD. Imaging revealed multiple hepatic lesions consistent with HCAs, prompting further genetic evaluation. Trio exome sequencing identified biallelic variants in the glucose-6-phophatase gene, confirming a diagnosis of glycogen storage disease type Ia (GSD Ia). This case highlights the diagnostic challenge posed by overlapping features of MASLD and GSD Ia, particularly hepatic steatosis, HCAs, and metabolic syndrome. Initial management of MASLD with glucagon-like peptide-1 therapy was discontinued given risk for hypoglycemia, and the patient continues glucose monitoring and cornstarch therapy. This case emphasizes the importance of including inborn errors of metabolism in the differential diagnosis for multifocal HCAs and concerns with obesity treatments.

title: Pharmacotherapy for MASLD: current evidence and challenges in clinical practice.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is characterized by a complex pathophysiology driven by intertwined metabolic and hepatic pathways, enabling the identification of multiple therapeutic targets and a rapidly expanding drug development pipeline. This review summarizes the current and emerging therapeutic landscape for MASLD and discusses key challenges for clinical implementation. The imminent availability of several new therapies is expected to pose important clinical challenges, particularly in accurately identifying patients most likely to benefit. Currently, resmetirom and semaglutide are the only two drugs conditionally approved for patients with fibrosis stages 2-3, pending final phase 3 outcomes, and represent the main liver-directed and metabolic-focused therapeutic strategies, respectively. Treatment selection should follow a phenotype-based approach integrating metabolic profile and liver disease stage. Non-invasive tests are central for assessing treatment eligibility; however, strategies incorporating metabolic risk profiling and longitudinal monitoring will be essential to optimize real-world management of MASH.

title: Transient Adipose Inflammatory Remodeling during High-Dose Semaglutide-Induced Weight Loss and Regain.
abstract: Weight loss improves obesity-associated metabolic dysfunction, yet resolution of adipose inflammation may be incomplete and can reappear during weight regain. Whether high-dose semaglutide induces sustained immunological remodeling of adipose and hepatic tissues during weight cycling remains unclear. Male C57BL/6 mice with diet-induced obesity were treated with semaglutide (60 nmol/kg, intraperitoneally, every 3 days) or vehicle for 3 weeks, followed by drug withdrawal under continued high-fat diet feeding. Body weight, body composition, and glucose homeostasis were assessed during treatment and after weight regain. Inflammatory changes in visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue and liver were analyzed by flow cytometry, histology, immunofluorescence, and gene expression profiling. Semaglutide induced rapid fat mass-selective weight loss with preservation of lean mass and significantly improved fasting glucose, insulin levels, insulin sensitivity, and glucose tolerance. During treatment, visceral adipose tissue exhibited marked reductions in pro-inflammatory macrophages, crown-like structures, and inflammatory gene expression, whereas subcutaneous adipose tissue was minimally affected. Following withdrawal, mice rapidly regained weight and adiposity. Visceral adipose inflammation fully reverted, with macrophage infiltration and inflammatory gene expression comparable to chronically obese controls. Hepatic steatosis and inflammatory markers similarly returned to obese levels. Despite this tissue-level reversion, fasting glycemia and insulin levels remained partially improved. High-dose semaglutide induces robust metabolic improvement and transient suppression of visceral adipose inflammation during active treatment; however, these inflammatory changes are not sustained after withdrawal and largely revert with weight regain. In contrast, partial improvement in fasting glycemia persisted, suggesting differential durability between systemic metabolic adaptation and local inflammatory remodeling during pharmacological weight cycling.

title: Endocrine determinants of MASLD: mechanisms and therapeutic targets.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects approximately 30% of adults worldwide, yet is still framed largely as a hepatological disorder despite being driven substantially by endocrine and metabolic dysfunction. This review proposes a unified endocrine framework organised around seven hormonal axes, presenting each in terms of molecular pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and therapeutic implications. Insulin resistance is the central driver, coupling chronic caloric excess to hepatic de novo lipogenesis through selective hepatic insulin resistance, although genetic variants in PNPLA3 and TM6SF2 can uncouple steatosis from metabolic risk. Adipose tissue dysfunction contributes through adipocyte senescence, adipokine imbalance, and inflammatory adipose-liver signalling. Reduced hepatic thyroid hormone sensitivity, even in euthyroid individuals, predicts steatosis and fibrosis and underpins the first approved liver-directed therapy. Gonadal steroids exert sexually dimorphic effects, with testosterone deficiency, menopausal oestrogen loss, and polycystic ovary syndrome representing distinct risk states. Glucocorticoid dysregulation is stage-dependent, shifting from enhanced hepatic cortisol clearance in steatosis to local amplification in steatohepatitis. The gut-liver-endocrine axis, encompassing incretin, bile acid, and fibroblast growth factor signalling, has proved the most therapeutically tractable. Reduced GH/IGF-1 signalling, whether from pituitary disease or obesity-induced functional suppression, promotes both steatosis and fibrogenesis. Biological sex and life-course influences spanning developmental programming and ageing further modify these determinants. Two agents, resmetirom and semaglutide, now have US FDA accelerated approval for noncirrhotic MASH with moderate-to-advanced fibrosis, supporting the principle that correcting axis-specific endocrine dysfunction can produce measurable hepatic benefit; however, both approvals are accelerated and await confirmatory outcome data, while others remain investigational. An endocrine framework offers both a coherent account of pathogenesis and a rational basis for biomarker-guided, phenotype-targeted therapy.

title: Evolving phenotype of newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes: a 15-year population-based comparison.
abstract: Our aim was to describe the phenotype at diagnosis and the early therapeutic profile of newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes across two periods spanning approximately 15 years within the same integrated healthcare system. This retrospective cohort study used electronic health record data from Clalit Health Services (Haifa & Western Galilee, Israel). Adults with incident type 2 diabetes in 2005-2008 (period 1: n=80,201) were compared with those diagnosed in 2020-2023 (period 2: n=101,392). Between-period differences are presented as crude estimates, with an age-stratified sensitivity analysis, and quantified using standardised mean differences (SMDs; values ≥0.20 indicate at least a small effect) alongside non-parametric and χ2 tests. The median age at diagnosis increased from 63.0 to 66.7 years between the two periods; the proportion aged ≥85 years nearly doubled (from 3.5% to 6.6%). The score for the Charlson comorbidity index increased from 4 to 6 (SMD 0.48); metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) increased from 4.4% to 18.6%. HbA1c at diagnosis decreased from 56 to 53 mmol/mol (7.3% to 7.0%); pre-diagnosis LDL-cholesterol decreased from 2.90 to 2.21 mmol/l (SMD 0.65). Within 31-90 days of diagnosis, use of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors increased from 0.07% to 15.0%, use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) increased from 0% to 11.1%, and sulfonylurea use decreased more than fourfold (20.8% to 4.5%). The phenotype of newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes has been fundamentally restructured since 2008: patients are older with a higher comorbidity burden but present with better glycaemic and lipid management, with the latter reflecting statin therapy already established before diagnosis. MASLD has emerged as a major but largely ascertainment-driven comorbidity. The shift to SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1RAs alongside declining sulfonylurea use indicates displacement of glucose-centric strategies by a cardiorenal- and weight-driven paradigm. These findings indicate a need for age-appropriate management and trials enrolling very elderly patients.

title: Dietary and Nutritional Considerations for Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease in Psoriasis and Hidradenitis Suppurativa: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is increasingly recognised in patients with chronic inflammatory skin disease, particularly psoriasis, for which epidemiological evidence of increased MASLD prevalence is relatively strong; corresponding data in hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) remain more limited. This narrative review examines the epidemiological and biological links between psoriasis, HS and MASLD, and evaluates dietary and nutritional strategies relevant to their multidisciplinary management. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing direct evidence in patients with concomitant inflammatory skin disease and MASLD from evidence derived from dermatology cohorts without liver-specific outcomes and from general MASLD populations. Mediterranean-style dietary patterns, energy restriction and weight loss, improved diet quality, and reduced intake of ultra-processed foods and added sugars are supported principally by MASLD and cardiometabolic data, with more limited direct evidence in psoriasis or HS. The review also discusses nutritional considerations during incretin-based therapy, including reduced food intake, preservation of lean mass, micronutrient adequacy and gastrointestinal adverse effects, while highlighting areas in which recommendations remain extrapolated or expert-derived. For dermatologists, the practical emphasis is on recognition of metabolic risk, general dietary counselling and appropriate multidisciplinary referral. Overall, nutritional management is an important component of MASLD care, but dedicated intervention studies in patients with concomitant psoriasis or HS remain a major evidence gap.

title: Canonical and Non-Canonical Regulators of Lipid Metabolism in the Liver and the "Liver-Other Organs" Axes.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the most common chronic liver disease and is closely associated with obesity, insulin resistance, and the recently conceptualized cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome. For decades, the pathogenesis of steatosis has been viewed primarily through the lens of insulin and the canonical transcriptional programs it regulates-sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1c, carbohydrate response element-binding protein, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors, and AMP-activated protein kinase. At the same time, recent data point to the existence of a complex network of non-canonical regulators that, independently of insulin, significantly modulate hepatic lipid metabolism. This review systematizes information on the fibroblast growth factors FGF21 and FGF19, adipokines (adiponectin, leptin), apolipoprotein C-III, as well as the monoamine neurotransmitters serotonin and dopamine. These molecules act within the interorgan axes "liver-adipose tissue," "gut-liver," "brain-liver," and "liver-spleen," coordinating lipolysis, gluconeogenesis, very-low-density lipoprotein secretion, inflammation, and fibrogenesis. Disruption of the dynamic balance between canonical and non-canonical regulators is central to the progression from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis and fibrosis. The clinical translation of this concept has already begun: the thyroid hormone receptor β agonist resmetirom and the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist semaglutide have received regulatory approval for specific categories of patients with noncirrhotic metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and fibrosis, while FGF21 and FGF19 analogs, the dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 agonist tirzepatide, and agents targeting apolipoprotein C-III are at various stages of clinical development or are being used for related metabolic indications. Expanding the insulin-centric paradigm to include non-canonical axes opens up new diagnostic and therapeutic possibilities for MASLD.

title: Potential Physiological Convergence Between GLP-1 Receptor Signaling and Hepatocyte TAZ in Metabolic Liver Disease: From Metabolic Homeostasis to Fibrotic Remodeling.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) progresses when nutrient excess, insulin resistance, adipose dysfunction, and hepatocellular stress overwhelm hepatic adaptation. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) improve weight, glycemic control, and steatohepatitis, and semaglutide has demonstrated histological improvement in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). In parallel, the transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ; WWTR1) has emerged as a nutrient-, cholesterol-, and mechanics-responsive regulator linking stressed hepatocytes to inflammation and fibrogenesis through Hippo-YAP/TAZ signaling and Indian hedgehog. This narrative review integrates incretin physiology with cell-specific TAZ biology across the gut-brain-axis, adipose tissue, pancreatic islets, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, hepatocytes, immune cells, and hepatic stellate cells. Recent evidence that semaglutide can signal through intrahepatic sinusoidal endothelial GLP-1 receptors provides a weight-loss-independent route to reduced hepatic inflammation and fibrosis; however, it does not establish that TAZ is a downstream mediator. The evidence therefore supports a multilevel convergence model in which GLP-1RAs lower metabolic and inflammatory inputs that favor TAZ activation, while direct GLP-1RA-to-TAZ signaling remains a testable hypothesis. Receptor-validated, cell-specific, weight-controlled, and longitudinal human studies are needed to distinguish mediation from parallel response and to determine whether TAZ-pathway biomarkers can guide mechanism-based therapy.

title: MetALD in Clinical Practice: Diagnosis, Non-Invasive Risk Stratification, and Management.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease with increased alcohol consumption (MetALD) is a newly defined category within the spectrum of steatotic liver disease. It captures patients who have both cardiometabolic risk factors and alcohol intake above the thresholds accepted for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). This overlap matters clinically, as the coexistence of metabolic dysfunction and increased alcohol exposure is associated with a higher risk of progressive liver disease. In this narrative review, we bring together current evidence on the diagnosis, non-invasive risk stratification, and management of MetALD, with particular attention to serum-based fibrosis scores such as the Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index and imaging-based methods including vibration-controlled transient elastography and controlled attenuation parameter. We also consider the factors that can complicate the interpretation of these non-invasive tests when alcohol use is ongoing. Management has to address both components of the disease at once: reducing alcohol exposure, treating alcohol use disorder where present, managing weight, and controlling cardiometabolic risk factors. Incretin-based therapies are attracting growing interest given their established metabolic effects and the emerging hepatic and alcohol-related data, though no randomized trial has yet tested their efficacy specifically in MetALD. In advanced disease, liver transplantation remains the definitive option for appropriately selected patients, but it requires careful assessment of cardiometabolic comorbidities, alcohol-related risk, and frailty. Further prospective studies are needed to clarify the natural history of MetALD, define optimal risk-stratification strategies, and establish treatment outcomes in this population.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonist and Gastrointestinal Adverse Effects: A Comprehensive Review.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) has transformed the management of type 2 diabetes and obesity, with expanding indications now spanning cardiovascular, renal, and hepatic disease. As exposure broadens across increasingly diverse populations, gastrointestinal adverse events (GIAEs) have emerged as the dominant tolerability limitation and a leading drug-related reason for discontinuation of treatment. This review synthesizes the mechanisms, clinical spectrum, and management of GLP-1 RA-associated GIAEs. These effects arise from a dual peripheral-central mechanism: peripheral receptor activation slows gastric motility, whereas activation in the area postrema and nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) drives nausea and emesis. This dual mechanism explains why symptom severity may correlate poorly with the measured degree of gastric-emptying delay and why centrally acting antiemetics are most widely used to relieve nausea and emesis. Across clinical trials, nausea, emesis, diarrhea, constipation, and abdominal pain follow a consistent dose- and indication-dependent gradient, with the highest incidence observed with higher-dose obesity and MASH regimens and multi-agonist molecules. Most symptoms are mild, emerge during dose escalation, and attenuate over time, though a clinically important minority of patients experience persistent symptoms, and a subset develops gastroparesis. Management should rest on anticipation and screening of gastrointestinal symptoms at baseline, pretreatment counseling, gradual up-titration, and dietary measures before pharmacotherapy. Future priorities include standardized motility measurements and endpoints, predictive biomarkers, and evidence-based management algorithms.

title: Differential functions of ROCK1 and ROCK2 in liver fibrosis and advances in targeted therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Liver fibrosis, driven by metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and other chronic injuries, represents a global health crisis without approved pharmacological therapies. The Rho-associated coiled-coil kinases (ROCK1 and ROCK2), the principal effectors of Rho GTPases, have emerged as central nodes in fibrogenesis, yet the isoform-specific mechanisms and their translational potential remain incompletely defined. This review systematically dissects the divergent roles of ROCK1 and ROCK2 across the hepatic cellular landscape. We synthesize current knowledge on isoform-specific functions across major hepatic cell types, including hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs), hepatocytes, macrophages, and immune cells, with emphasis on the evidence quality underlying each claim. ROCK2 appears to play a predominant role in the profibrotic vascular niche in several contexts, particularly in LSEC capillarization and HSC contraction; however, the contributions of both isoforms are fundamentally cell- and context-dependent. We discuss the evidence for ROCK isoform-specific functions, distinguishing among genetic, pharmacological, expression-based, and activation-based evidence. We further synthesize the complex crosstalk between ROCK signaling and the TGF-β/Smad, Wnt/β-catenin, Hippo/YAP, and NOX4/ROS networks. Crucially, we critically evaluate the translational pipeline-from pan-ROCK inhibitors limited by systemic hypotension to next-generation selective ROCK2 inhibitors. A notable development in clinical translation is the selective ROCK2 inhibitor TDI01, which targets endothelial ROCK2 to attenuate fibrosis. In an extended, single-arm, open-label study of TDI01 in patients with liver fibrosis, fibrosis improvement was observed in five of six patients; however, given the small sample size, absence of a control group, and exploratory endpoints, these findings represent early signals that require validation in adequately powered randomized controlled trials. We further address unresolved controversies, including the dual hepatoprotective versus pro-steatotic functions of ROCK and the dose-dependent bidirectional regulation of HSCs migration, which challenge systemic inhibition strategies. Looking forward, we spotlight emerging frontiers such as cell-specific nanodelivery systems (vitamin A-liposomes, M6PHSA), PROTAC-mediated ROCK degradation, non-coding RNA therapeutics, and synergistic combinations with FXR, PPAR, and GLP-1 receptor agonists. This review provides a comprehensive blueprint for translating ROCK isoform biology into precision antifibrotic therapies.

title: Pharmacotherapy for MASLD/MASH: approved therapies, drug repurposing, and emerging mechanism-based candidates.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASLD/MASH) pharmacotherapy is changing rapidly after the approval of resmetirom and semaglutide for selected adults with noncirrhotic MASH and F2-F3 fibrosis; management must also address obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, cardiovascular risk, and kidney disease. This structured narrative review evaluates approved, comorbidity-directed, repurposed, and emerging therapies according to mechanism, regulatory status, endpoint strength, safety, interactions, and implementation. PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched without a lower date limit through September 2026 and supplemented by U.S. and European regulatory documents, society guidance, randomized trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and selected mechanistic studies. Therapies include thyroid hormone receptor-beta agonism, incretin and glucagon-containing agonists, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor pathways, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibition, de novo lipogenesis/fatty acid synthase inhibition, fibroblast growth factor 21 analogues, lipid/remnant pharmacology, farnesoid X receptor signaling, antioxidants, and lower-evidence repurposing candidates. Resmetirom and semaglutide anchor approved MASH-directed treatment in eligible F2-F3 disease, while comorbidity-directed therapy should be individualized by liver stage and cardiometabolic priorities. Tirzepatide, FGF21 analogues, denifanstat, and rational combinations may broaden treatment, but cross-trial comparisons and surrogate endpoints require cautious interpretation.

title: Transgenerational effects of paternal in utero arsenic exposure on MASLD-like phenotypes.
abstract: Previous study indicated that early-life arsenic (As) exposure caused adulthood metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)-like phenotypes. This study aimed to investigate the impacts of paternal in utero As exposure on MASLD-like phenotypes in offspring. Pregnant dams received NaAsO2 (15 mg/L) through drinking water. In utero As-exposed male pups were designated as F0 mice and mated with untreated females to produce F1 offspring. F1 males were subsequently mated with untreated females to generate F2 offspring, both without further As exposure. MASLD-like phenotypes were evaluated in F1 and F2 offspring. On PNW28, As-exposed F1 offspring exhibited hepatic steatosis, glucose intolerance, insulin resistance, and obesity, accompanied by altered metabolic hormones, such as GLP-1, GIP, insulin, leptin, and ADPN. The core MASLD-like phenotypes, including hepatic steatosis, glucose intolerance and insulin resistance, exhibited transgenerational transmission from F1 to F2 generations. In F2 offspring, these metabolic abnormalities were detected at PNW45 but not at PNW28, predominantly in male offspring. In contrast, As-induced obesity and metabolic hormone alterations exhibited transgenerational attenuation. F2 offspring retained only adipocyte hypertrophy, with no significant changes in white or brown adipose tissue weight. Furthermore, hormonal alterations in F2 mice were limited to reduced GLP-1 levels in females and elevated insulin and ADPN levels in males, while other altered hormones normalized. This study is the first to confirm that paternal in utero As exposure causes MASLD-like phenotypes in F1 offspring and transgenerational transmission to F2 generation.

title: Tirzepatide use in adolescents with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD): A case series.
abstract: Pediatric obesity and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) prevalence has risen markedly over the past decade. Due to transition delays and workforce shortages, pediatric specialists often manage patients into young adulthood, and thus familiarity with adult pharmacotherapies for MASLD is essential. Currently, Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, is approved for adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and F2-F3 fibrosis; however, dual and triple agonists are being evaluated. Tirzepatide, a dual agonist that targets gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) and the GLP-1 receptor, has demonstrated superior weight reduction to Semaglutide (-20.2% vs. -13.7%) with a more favorable gastrointestinal adverse effect profile. Adult literature has demonstrated its effectiveness in MASH resolution, and pediatric data suggest it is safe in younger populations. Currently, there are no pediatric/adolescent studies exploring the use of Tirzepatide in MASLD. We present our experience using Tirzepatide in two adolescent patients with obesity and MASLD.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis: protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a major global chronic liver disease without approved pharmacotherapy. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) show therapeutic promise due to their multi-faceted metabolic benefits, but their efficacy on histological endpoints in MASH requires definitive synthesis. We will conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating GLP-1 RAs versus placebo/standard care in adults with MASH. Literature searches will be performed in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science. Two reviewers will independently screen studies, extract data, and assess risk of bias using Cochrane's ROB 2 tool. The primary outcome is histological improvement (MASH resolution/fibrosis reduction). Secondary outcomes include changes in liver enzymes, metabolic parameters, and adverse events. Data will be pooled using random-effects models. Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA) will be performed to control random errors and evaluate evidence robustness. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses are planned. Ethical approval is not required because this study is a secondary analysis of existing data. We will disseminate the findings through peer- reviewed publications. PROSPERO CRD420261287573.

title: Alcohol consumption: from biochemistry to behavior, health, and beyond.
abstract: Alcohol metabolism is a multi-step biochemical process driven primarily by hepatic oxidation of ethanol to acetaldehyde and then to acetate. Although this pathway protects the body from prolonged ethanol exposure, transient acetaldehyde accumulation generates substantial toxicity, and chronic alcohol intake activates auxiliary pathways that amplify oxidative stress, inflammation, and tissue injury. Both metabolic capacity and physiological response to alcohol vary widely between individuals, reflecting genetic and epigenetic variation in the alcohol- and aldehyde-dehydrogenase enzymes, the cytochrome P450 system, and modulating factors such as sex, age, body composition, nutrition, and overall health. In this review we consolidate 3 decades of biochemical, clinical, and epidemiological evidence into an integrated picture of alcohol's effects on the liver, brain, and other organ systems, with attention to oxidative stress, neurochemistry, glycoconjugate biology, and the convergence of alcohol- and metabolic-driven liver disease. We also examine recent advances in the treatment of alcohol use disorder (AUD) - including incretin-based pharmacotherapies, ketamine-assisted therapy, focused ultrasound neuromodulation, exercise interventions, and combination drug regimens - and we critically evaluate ongoing controversies surrounding moderate drinking, resveratrol, and the use of heterogeneous non-drinker comparison groups in observational studies. Finally, we discuss the changing social context of drinking, the role of endogenous ethanol/acetaldehyde systems in stress resilience across species, and the implications of these insights for personalized prevention and risk-reduction strategies. We conclude by proposing an exposure-susceptibility-context model that integrates the principal determinants of alcohol-related harm.

title: The Power of Two: Harnessing Dual Glucagon and Incretin Signaling for Treatment of Obesity and Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatohepatitis-A Narrative Review with a Translational Focus.
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity
abstract: A resurgence in glucagon research has repositioned this pancreatic hormone as a promising target in the treatment of obesity and related metabolic disorders. Glucagon is classically known for contributing to glucose homeostasis, but emerging evidence points to a much wider role in metabolism, including energy balance and liver health. These findings are fueling attempts to understand how to leverage glucagon signaling to treat obesity and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). Due to potential hyperglycemic effects of glucagon signaling, most investigational compounds are dual agonists of both the glucagon and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptors to harness the antihyperglycemic and anorectic effects of the latter hormone, analogs of which such as semaglutide are already proven to be potent obesity medications. Glucagon receptor/GLP-1 receptor dual agonists reduce food intake, decrease hepatic fat, and increase energy expenditure in animal models of obesity and MASH. In early clinical trials, some dual agonists substantially reduced body weight, hepatic steatosis, and hepatic fibrosis. Whether they are more effective than GLP-1 receptor mono-agonists remains to be established in definitive head-to-head studies. The precise balance between glucagon and GLP-1 signaling within individual compounds appears important for overall therapeutic effects-including glycemic control, which worsened with some dual agonists. However, the two most clinically advanced compounds-mazdutide (approved for chronic weight management and type 2 diabetes in China) and survodutide (ongoing global phase 3 trials)-had potent weight-loss and antihyperglycemic effects in people with obesity, with survodutide also improving liver health in people with MASH. Therefore, the research into glucagon physiology that led to glucagon receptor/GLP-1 receptor dual agonists is translating to advantageous new therapies for the highly prevalent diseases of obesity and MASH.

title: Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease: redefining the conceptual framework from nomenclature to emerging therapeutic paradigms.
abstract: The renaming of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) to metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD), and subsequently to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), signals a paradigm shift that repositions hepatic steatosis as a systemic metabolic disorder rather than a diagnosis by exclusion. This review synthesizes the evidence supporting the nomenclature transition, examines the pathogenic mechanisms driving disease progression, evaluates the clinical implications of the lean MAFLD phenotype, and surveys the evolving therapeutic landscape. Oxidative stress, chronic low-grade inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction form an interconnected network propelling the trajectory from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis and fibrosis. The bidirectional liver-adipose tissue communication axis, modulated by micronutrient homeostasis, has emerged as an integrative framework for understanding disease pathobiology. Lean MAFLD, present in 20-40% of affected individuals despite normal body mass index, challenges obesity-centered screening approaches and underscores the necessity of metabolic phenotyping in routine clinical practice. Extrahepatic complications-particularly subclinical cardiovascular injury, type 2 diabetes-associated hepatocellular carcinoma, and cardiomyopathy-remain the principal causes of death in this population. The regulatory approval of resmetirom in March 2024, together with promising phase II data on incretin-based therapies, FGF21 analogs, and PPAR modulators, has begun to reshape a therapeutic field that had long relied on lifestyle modification alone. We also discuss the gut-liver axis, genetic predisposition, economic burden, and multidisciplinary management models that together define the contemporary understanding of this disease. This review integrates these developments and identifies key gaps warranting further investigation.

title: The PTPN1/N2 Peptide Inhibitor Achieves Potent, Long-Acting Glycemic Control and Weight-Loss Dual Efficacy in Mice.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity are closely linked metabolic disorders driven by insulin and leptin resistance. Current long-acting therapies capable of addressing both conditions are dominated by incretin-based agents, which primarily achieve efficacy through appetite suppression and are frequently associated with tolerability limitations and metabolic rebound after treatment discontinuation. Alternative strategies that correct underlying signaling defects without suppressing food intake remain lacking. Protein tyrosine phosphatases PTPN1 and PTPN2 act as coordinated intracellular negative regulators of insulin and leptin signaling by dephosphorylating key molecules within the IRS-AKT and JAK2-STAT3 pathways. Although genetic studies have established these phosphatases as attractive therapeutic targets, translation has been hindered by the absence of long-acting inhibitors with robust in vivo efficacy. Here we report the rational design of Y5, a chemically engineered BimBH3-derived peptide analogue that functions as a dual inhibitor of PTPN1 and PTPN2. Fatty-acid conjugation and hapten modification confer high enzymatic potency, enhanced proteolytic stability, strong albumin binding, and prolonged half-life and systemic exposure. Y5 restores cellular insulin and leptin signaling in vitro, leading to coordinated activation of IRS-1, AKT, and STAT3 under resistant conditions. In diabetic db/db mice, Y5 once-weekly administration induces sustained glycemic control, improves glucose tolerance, and reduces circulating insulin levels, consistent with enhanced insulin sensitivity. In DIO mice, Y5 induces pronounced and sustained weight loss while preserving food intake, demonstrating a potential mechanism distinct from incretin-based therapies. Y5 selectively reduces adiposity, improves hepatic steatosis, and is well tolerated across dosing regimens. These findings establish long-acting dual inhibition of PTPN1 and PTPN2 as a mechanistically distinct therapeutic strategy for T2DM and obesity.
